lesson.title: Beyond Fixing What's Wrong: The Positive Psychology Movement
lesson.summary: Positive psychology is the scientific study of the strengths, positive emotions, and conditions that allow individuals and communities to flourish, not only the study of what goes wrong.
lesson.body:
For most of the twentieth century, psychology's clinical and research energy was directed overwhelmingly toward understanding and treating dysfunction: mental illness, trauma, disorder. In 1998, Martin Seligman, during his term as president of the American Psychological Association, argued that this focus had left the field lopsided. Psychology had become remarkably good at understanding suffering and comparatively silent on what makes a life good. That address is widely credited with launching positive psychology as an organized area of study.

Positive psychology asks a different kind of question than clinical psychology traditionally has. Instead of "what is broken and how do we fix it," it asks "what is working, and how can we build more of it." Seligman later organized much of this thinking around a model he called PERMA: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment, five elements he proposed each contribute independently to a flourishing life, not just to fleeting happiness.

It is worth being clear about what positive psychology is not. It is not a call to simply think positively or to ignore pain and hardship. It uses the same empirical, hypothesis-testing methods found across the rest of the field, the same commitment to psychology as a rigorous science, and applies that rigor to questions about well-being rather than only to questions about disorder. The field also has intellectual roots that predate its formal naming: humanistic psychologists like Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow were writing about growth, potential, and self-actualization decades before positive psychology existed as a labeled subfield, and their work is often considered an important precursor.

The link to health psychology is direct. Health psychology had already established that mental states shape physical outcomes, that stress, coping style, and outlook influence disease risk and recovery. Positive psychology extended that same logic in the other direction, asking not only how negative states harm health but whether positive states, hope, optimism, strong social connection, might actively protect it. Later chapters in this unit look closely at specific outcomes this field studies, including well-being, resilience, gratitude, and personal strengths.
